abstract: Dense 3D tracking from monocular video requires establishing point correspondences over time, estimating their depth, and inferring their trajectories during occlusion. Existing methods typically learn these tasks jointly, a demanding objective given the scarcity of 4D supervision. We show that strong pretrained 2D trackers and 3D geometry models provide an effective foundation: lifted trajectories, with occluded segments simply interpolated, already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. However, lifted trajectories inherit correspondence and depth errors, and under occlusion, their depth comes from the occluder rather than the tracked point. We introduce ReLift, an efficient feed-forward framework that recasts dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion. At its core, a trajectory corrector alternates attention along and across trajectories to preserve reliable observations, repair corrupted positions, and complete missing motion. Using only geometric inputs allows us to train directly on 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, decoupling training from images and from any specific tracker or geometry model. Concentrating 4D supervision on trajectory refinement yields a reusable model that consistently improves lifted trajectories across trackers and geometry providers without retraining, so it benefits directly from future advances in either component. On WorldTrack, ReLift achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points, with faster configurations remaining competitive with leading 3D trackers while running $2.7\text{--}4.4\times$ faster than 4RC. Visit our project page for more examples and code.

sections.body: The paper argues that dense monocular 3D tracking should not learn correspondence, depth and occluded motion jointly. The method takes each point's viewing ray from a 2D tracker and its range from a depth model, forming a lifted 3D trajectory. Occluded samples are discarded and gaps are filled by interpolation. The authors report that these initialized lifts can match or exceed the mean accuracy of learned 3D trackers using the same geometry (Tables 1 and 2). The remaining errors are depth-boundary jumps, jitter and missing motion during occlusion, which a compact corrector repairs. Training uses simulated lifting errors on PointOdyssey trajectories. The same weights transfer to six tracker–geometry combinations without retraining (Fig. 3).
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Monocular dense 3D tracking can focus learning on repair and completion because pretrained 2D trackers and geometry models already handle correspondence and depth.

sections.body: Classical non-rigid structure-from-motion and per-video optimization methods reconstruct dynamic 3D scenes from monocular video but need lengthy per-scene optimization. Shape of Motion, MoSca, Uni4D and TrackingWorld combine pretrained depth and tracking cues this way. Feed-forward geometry models such as VGGT, Depth Anything 3 and MonST3R estimate depth and cameras. 2D trackers including CoTracker, AllTracker and CoWTracker establish correspondences. Dense feed-forward 3D trackers, including DELTAv2, SpatialTrackerV2 and 4RC, predict trajectories directly. The authors position ReLift as a feed-forward combination of these components that learns residuals on tracks already lifted with pretrained depth and cameras.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior methods fit 3D tracks with per-scene optimization or learn them feed-forward, while ReLift reuses 2D tracks and frozen geometry.

sections.body: The method lifts each 2D track into 3D using a viewing ray from the tracker and a range from depth. Observations are masked with a tracker-specific visibility threshold, and gaps are filled by linear interpolation. Each track becomes a sequence of ray–point tokens grouped into chunks of C frames. The corrector processes groups of P tracks with alternating temporal attention along each track and across-track attention within each chunk. A prediction head outputs XYZ residuals that are added to the initialized trajectories. The stated attention cost is lower than joint attention over all tokens. Training uses only geometric inputs: randomized corruptions of PointOdyssey trajectories, with no images and no tracker or geometry model run.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: A trajectory corrector alternates temporal and across-track attention to predict 3D residuals on lifted trajectories.

sections.body: Table 1 reports 3D accuracy on WorldTrack after RANSAC Sim(3) alignment, averaged over four datasets. With CoWTracker and 4RC geometry, the corrector reaches a mean of 89.01 on all points and 86.95 on dynamic points. 4RC's own predictions reach 86.94 and 81.60 on the same two sets. With AllTracker and VGGT-Ω, mean all-point accuracy is 86.57 and runtime is 7.3 seconds. The 4RC baseline runs in 31.8 seconds, and the CoWTracker and 4RC configuration of the corrector runs in 40.4 seconds, so it is not the fastest configuration. Table 2 shows that removing wrong-surface corruptions causes the largest drop in gains over the initialized lift.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On WorldTrack, the corrector with CoWTracker and 4RC geometry reaches 89.01 mean all-point accuracy, above 4RC's 86.94.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that pretrained 2D tracks lifted with estimated geometry and gap initialization already rival dedicated 3D trackers under matched geometry. One corrector, trained on simulated lifting errors, improves all evaluated tracker–geometry combinations without retraining. The largest gains are on occluded points. The authors report the highest mean accuracy on WorldTrack among the compared methods, and faster configurations that stay competitive at lower runtime. They state that performance remains sensitive to input geometry (Appendix C.1). Handling geometric and persistent correspondence errors is left to future work.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Performance still depends on input geometry, and handling persistent correspondence errors is left to future work.

sections.body: The appendix gives implementation and evaluation details. Preprocessing uses visibility thresholds of 0.85 for AllTracker and 0.65 for CoWTracker. The corrector has 8 factorized attention blocks, width 384 and 19.1 M parameters (Table 3). Training uses 100 PointOdyssey scenes (6,137 windows) and 8 validation scenes. Corruption distributions are in Table 4. Evaluation covers 199 WorldTrack clips after one ADT clip is excluded, and baseline settings are in Table 5. Run time and peak memory at three resolutions are in Table 15. Additional ablations and qualitative comparisons appear in Figures 6 to 9.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists preprocessing, architecture, training corruptions, evaluation protocol, baseline configurations and runtime measurements.
